lines: Nick Root was Hunter's older brother.
He was gone at 27, taken by cancer.
The first of the solo records was Run With The Hunt.
Jam, grunge, and acoustic rock out of Manheim, PA.
Hunter was a founding member of SEEDS.
Which became Medusa's Disco due to trademarks.
Run With The Hunt was Hunter's first solo record.
A transitional piece to his modern solo career.
Inspired by other's talents, Emotions, Thoughts, Existence, Pain.
— Hunter Root, Blue Harvest Beat, 2014
We're musically Influenced by: Led Zeppelin, Nirvana, The Doors
— Hunter Root, Blue Harvest Beat, 2014
Favorite midnight snack: "Cereal."
Alex: cold pizza. Wynton: frozen food. Tyler: a Nutella-banana sandwich.
Wynton's Dad's living room was the first time we played together as a 4-piece band.
— Alex Aument, Blue Harvest Beat, 2014
First song the band ever played together: "Strange Chemistry"
— Tyler, Blue Harvest Beat, 2014
We chose "Questioned By A Ghost" because our super fan Nathan Reinsmith misheard a lyric on our hidden track "Medicine"
— Tyler, Blue Harvest Beat, 2014
Park Bench Pigeons — It's growth from my solo album version to the SEEDS creation
Hunter, Wynton and Tyler all had solo albums before SEEDS.
Wynton Huddle listed Queens of the Stone Age, Butthole Surfers, Nirvana, Primus, Syd Barrett-era Pink Floyd, Incubus and Miles Davis, and said the list could go on.
— Blue Harvest Beat, 2014
Hunter Root named two albums that reward repeat listening: Queens Of The Stone Age's Like Clockwork and Incubus's A Crow Left Of The Murder.
— Blue Harvest Beat, 2014
Hunter's vocals channel a pre-needle Cobain with Morrison appreciation.
— Harrison Giza, Blue Harvest Beat, 2014
The solos are just the right amount of melting face you need in your morning coffee.
— Harrison Giza, Blue Harvest Beat, 2014
In August 2014 the band had been together about a year and a half.
Conceived in Lancaster County — Hunter's words to Blue Harvest Beat.
Wynton came up with the main riff in our friend's garage… The band was not formed at this point in time.
— Hunter Root, Blue Harvest Beat, 2014
Medusa's first show was the main stage of the Chameleon Club in Lancaster… This was before we even had a bassist!
— Wynton Huddle, Chasing Destino, 2018
It was our second year in a row attending it and was even better than last year!
— Wynton Huddle, Chasing Destino, 2018
We don't suck. You won't hate us.
— Wynton Huddle, Chasing Destino, 2018
Hunter had an infatuation with cacti, but after pulling some needles out of his butt he's been less than eager.
— Wynton Huddle, Chasing Destino, 2018
We do indeed. It's not an easy balancing act, but we will all do whatever we must to keep the ball rolling!
— Wynton Huddle, Chasing Destino, 2018
We went from engineer to engineer and bassist to bassist trying to find the right thing. The solution for both things was in the same person.
— Wynton Huddle, LancasterOnline, 2019
I was not expecting to find [our market] in the PA festival scene… we break the monotony up a little bit.
— Wynton Huddle, LancasterOnline, 2019
some of the songs have a new, rawer energy from that experience
— Justin Wohlfeil, LancasterOnline, 2019
I'm a really big fan of memes, so I'm glad to follow the page and see what people come up with; it gets me going.
— Alex Aument, LancasterOnline, 2019
The fans already know every single word to songs because we've been playing them for so long, and they're not even out yet
— Wynton Huddle, LancasterOnline, 2019
When people leave a show, we just want them to feel liberated and refreshed.
— Wynton Huddle, LancasterOnline, 2019
Orphic Grimoire was recorded in Justin Wohlfeil's studio inside the Chameleon Club.
The band hunkered down there from October 2018, in frequent four-hour sessions.
August 2019 — Medusa's Disco opened for Godsmack at Allentown's Musikfest.
Their biggest crowd yet.
Fans ran a dedicated Facebook group: "Medusa's Discult."
~550 members in 2019 — per LNP, the only Lancaster band with its own fan group.
A Who tribute set at "Dam Stock" in Austin, PA went so well it became a live recording.
Plus a second Who-centric show at Tellus360, Nov 8, 2019.
I am Pennsylvania raised but I was born in Fayetteville, Arkansas. My brother and I both.
— Hunter Root, Whiskey Riff, 2023
The main reason it's titled this is for my older brother, Nicholas Root… He would love this name and would completely get it, being born there means a lot to us both.
— Hunter Root, Whiskey Riff, 2023
Nick passed away two years ago as of April 15th at the age of 27. I was 26 when he died. He played guitar before me and is the reason I picked it up to begin with.
— Hunter Root, Whiskey Riff, 2023
One of his worries on his deathbed was that he wouldn't be remembered when he was gone. Fuck that, this one is forever for you Nick, I wouldn't be here without you!
— Hunter Root, Whiskey Riff, 2023
If you haven't heard of Hunter Root yet, I suggest you change that.
— Hill Douglas, Whiskey Riff, 2023
This guy is the real deal, so you're going to want to mark your calendars for this one.
— Hill Douglas, Whiskey Riff, 2023
"Town Rat Heathen" dropped in January 2023 and went viral.
Nearly a million Spotify streams inside four months.
I started playing drums and guitar at the age of twelve because of my older brother, Nick. He was a guitar player and was my first true inspiration to pick up an instrument.
— Hunter Root, MuzicNotez, 2024
My first influences were classic rock bands that my father listened to… The Rolling Stones, Led Zeppelin, The Doors, Lynyrd Skynyrd
— Hunter Root, MuzicNotez, 2024
Since I was a boy I just wanted to be able to make honest music for a living. That has always been my dream.
— Hunter Root, MuzicNotez, 2024
I don't think music in itself has goals. The true point of music is simply the music itself.
— Hunter Root, MuzicNotez, 2024
My favorite concert was probably the time I saw "Fuzz" at Underground Arts in Philly
— Hunter Root, MuzicNotez, 2024
"Arkansas" has strong folky, country, southern rock roots that permeate the whole record.
— Hunter Root, MuzicNotez, 2024
I released a twenty second clip on Tiktok of me singing and playing the first verse. It got 500k views which prompted me to finish the song and release it immediately.
— Hunter Root, MuzicNotez, 2024
I went from 400 monthly listeners to 100k in a few months. It's over 3M plays on Spotify now.
"It is completely surreal… I feel blessed." — MuzicNotez, January 2024
you have way more time and freedom to do things at your own leisure. Art is sensitive so not being rushed affects the product tremendously.
— Hunter Root on recording solo, MuzicNotez, 2024
I just want to thank all my friends and fans pre-viral for helping me get to this point… You know who you are. And thank you to the new fans, Much love.
— Hunter Root, MuzicNotez, 2024
The songs weren't written to deliver a message. They're simply confessions set to music.
— Hunter Root, Shore Fire Media, 2025
Crooked Home was produced by Anders Osborne and engineered by David Kalmusky.
Cut at Addiction Studios, Nashville; released October 17, 2025 via Tolok.
Chad Cromwell — Neil Young's and Mark Knopfler's drummer — plays on Crooked Home.
With Marc Rogers on bass and keys, and Lindsay Lou's backing vocals on two tracks.
The "'94" single art is a childhood photo of Hunter and Nick.
Taken outside their dad's truck.
If you had to make up a name for a rocking but acoustic artist who tells straightforward stories without pathos, "Hunter Root" would fit the bill exactly.
— Isthmus, 2025
While the songs are in part a tribute to Root's brother, who died in 2021, the album isn't a downer.
— Isthmus, 2025
"Friendly Fire" was the third single off Crooked Home.
Born from a fallout with close friends.
The Crooked Home tour opened October 10, 2025, at The Abbey Bar in Harrisburg.
Then New York, Philadelphia, Boston, Nashville, Chicago and more.
Crooked Home is a personal reckoning that tells the story of my life, a life shaped by loss, addiction, and illness.
— Hunter Root, Shore Fire Media, 2025
I think a lot of folks listen to my music because it helps them through tough times. If there is anything I hope this album has to offer, it's that — a little bit of light.
— Hunter Root, Shore Fire Media, 2025
Crooked Home was the first record Hunter cut live with a full band.
In his whole career.
The album ran through vintage mics once used by Bob Dylan and Marianne Faithfull.
And reverb plates from Johnny Cash sessions.
"String Up a Necklace" is about a necklace his girlfriend made him.
To remind him of home while touring.
"My Brother's Bones" is a tribute to Nick.
Born of Hunter's wish to give his brother a proper resting place.
"Flash in the Pan" is about working-class hardship.
The divide between wealth and the lower-middle-class world Hunter grew up in.
Half the songs ended up being about my brother… '94' was almost the album title. It's the heart of it all.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
He was a heroin addict since he was about fifteen. He got sarcoma while he was living in Kensington, Philly… and he came home to die. I was there for the last six months of his life.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
He was doing hospice in our living room. It woke me up. When he died—only eleven months older than me—it felt like a piece of me went with him.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
I'd just run to my room, grab the guitar, and hide in music. That was my formula for dealing with stuff. It's a healthy habit I built early, and it's what's kept me alive.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
My brother's biggest fear was not being remembered. So it was obvious what I had to do: remember him through music. I didn't plan it out, but it became everything.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
That Bronco was huge for us. When my dad sold it after we moved back to Pennsylvania, my brother cried. It's in the ''94' video.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
Two weeks before he died, he wanted to go back to Kensington one last time to get high… Watching him wheel himself away, looking like a skeleton—it's burned in my brain.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
It made people cry. That's when I knew—it's my first truly sad song, intentionally sad… That's what they want from music, and that's what I want to give: honesty.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
He started playing guitar first, when he was eight. He's the reason I play. I wanted to be in a band with him. I wouldn't be doing any of this if it wasn't for him.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
The label put money into the record, but it's still just me being me. The quality's higher, but the goal's the same: to turn pain into something that matters.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
My brother was always running from something dark. I'm just trying to face it head-on through music. That's how I keep him alive. That's how I keep myself alive.
— Hunter Root, Americana Highways, 2025
Crooked Home was Hunter's first label-backed release.
At 30, based in Columbia, outside Lancaster.
For the first time ever, all I had to do was sing and play in real time. It was the best result I have ever had. More honest. More alive.
— Hunter Root, The Country Note, 2025
I have been playing music since I was twelve. I am just a full blooded musician. That is all I know how to do.
— Hunter Root, The Country Note, 2025
It's spelled Root — but pronounced "Rut."
The spelling stuck as the stage name; he says it suits the music's earthy tone.
I have always struggled to fit in genre wise. Every time I hear something new, it ends up in my music. I do not want to land anywhere because I like so many styles.
— Hunter Root, The Country Note, 2025
Arkansas was the first time I wrote real lines about real places and the things I actually did. And that is when people connected.
— Hunter Root, The Country Note, 2025
People were not just connecting with vague lines. They connected with the exact story. My dad in jail. My brother in rehab. The legal drug stuff.
— Hunter Root, The Country Note, 2025
If I was on a deserted island, I would just need my guitar and the ability to play a song all the way through. That is home for me.
— Hunter Root, The Country Note, 2025
This is my heart and soul. Not being able to tour weighs on me mentally. But I still have room to get better. I am not worried.
— Hunter Root, The Country Note, 2025
Everything I love about Hank, that is what people connect with in my music. That is wild to think about.
— Hunter Root, The Country Note, 2025
Struggle is struggle.
— Michelle Osterhoudt, The Country Note, 2025
A song he wishes he could hear again for the first time.
Nirvana's unplugged "Where Did You Sleep Last Night."
The lyric comes first now — it used to be the riff.
Notebook and pen; writing happens on the couch with the TV off, or on a long walk with coffee.
He grew up in Lancaster's Amish country.
Rural life plus psychedelic rock, grunge, and bluegrass shaped the sound.
The night after opening for Godsmack, Medusa's Disco closed the Peace of Mind series at Rt. 61 Roadhouse in Sunbury.
"They showed no signs of disinterest" — PA Musician's columnist.
"Book Upon My Shelf" landed August 14, 2019.
The band's first single in three years.
Medusa's Disco's songwriting is a quality that sets them apart from other bands.
— Sarah Kate Gittleman, NEPAudio, 2019
the album is a perfect snapshot of the energy that Medusa's Disco brings to listeners
— Sarah Kate Gittleman, NEPAudio, 2019
Orphic Grimoire — the band's fourth studio release.
Recorded, mixed, and produced entirely by Medusa's Disco.
"Belly Ache" carries a saxophone break by YAM YAM's Jason Mescia.
Woven into the instrumental breakdown.
On "Sizzle Into Oblivion": "it is nothing short of the stuff goosebumps are risen from."
The album closer — per the review, the most popular song among fans.
